## Cost to double (buy 170 more shares)

- **At your average cost ($42.12):** 170 × $42.12 = **$7,160.40**
- **At today's market (~$20.39):** 170 × $20.39 = **$3,466.30**

## Verdict: ✅ GO on affordability

Even the worst-case framing — paying full average cost of **$7,160.40** — is covered by your cash alone, using just **~11%** of your $66,493.59 checking+savings. You don't even need to touch the credit card's $1,649 headroom. At the real market price it's only ~$3,466, about 5% of liquid cash. One logistical note: your brokerage holds only $420 in cash, so you'd have to transfer funds from checking first before placing the order.

## ⚠️ Concentration-risk caveat (the reason to hesitate anyway)

Affordable ≠ advisable. This is the part that should give you pause:

- GME is already **~31.5%** of your $10,999.70 portfolio.
- Doubling it pushes GameStop to roughly **48% of the enlarged portfolio** — nearly half your money in a single ticker.
- That single name is a famously volatile meme stock currently sitting **‑51.59% below your entry**. A further leg down would hit close to half your net worth simultaneously, with no diversification cushion.
- Average-cost math also matters: adding 170 shares at today's lower price *would* meaningfully lower your blended average (from $42.12 toward ~$31), so it's a cheaper dollar-cost-average than buying at your original basis — but that only helps if you're confident in the thesis; it doesn't reduce the concentration itself.

**Bottom line:** Yes, you can comfortably afford it — cash covers it several times over with room to spare. But you'd be betting nearly half your portfolio on one high-volatility stock that's already cut in half for you. My suggestion if you proceed: size it down (e.g., add 50–85 shares rather than a full 170) so GME stays under ~35–40% of the portfolio, keep the emergency cash intact, and never fund equity purchases on the credit card given the interest will erode any gains.
